segments.title: Why a historian may omit a seminal work
segments.summary: A landmark secondary work may be omitted when the author relies on primary evidence and space is limited, or when citing it would manufacture controversy around a difference of interpretation.
segments.body: Two reasons can explain why an important book does not appear in a historian's source list. A bibliography and recommended-reading list cannot include every relevant secondary work because books still face word and page limits. If a section rests directly on primary sources and does not cite a particular secondary work, even an excellent book may be left out. The other reason arises when a famous study and a new book interpret the same evidence differently. A marketing team could present that difference as a dramatic claim that the new book disproves the old one. Some historians welcome that controversy, while others prefer to let a book stand on its own evidence and argument. Returning to the primary sources can keep a difference of analytical perspective from becoming a manufactured feud.
segments.question: Why would a historian omit a seminal work on the subject from the source list?
segments.answerShort: The work may not have been cited when primary sources carried the argument and space was limited, or the author may wish to avoid turning a difference of interpretation into an artificial controversy.

evidence.note: The video asks why a historian might omit a seminal work from the source list.
The first reason combines reliance on primary sources with finite word, page, and recommended-reading space.
The second reason concerns publicity that can follow a difference of analytical perspective.
Dr Clarke explains his preference for avoiding manufactured drama and working from the primary evidence.

segments.title: What makes a work seminal in naval history
segments.summary: Andrew Lambert, Norman Friedman, and D. K. Brown are examples of one generation's seminal naval scholarship. Nicholas Rodger and Andrew Boyd may become comparable reference points.
segments.body: Academic fields develop authors whose work becomes a reference point for a generation. In naval history, Andrew Lambert, Norman Friedman, and D. K. Brown are given as examples, and their books remain excellent even when a particular author does not cite them. Nicholas Rodger and Andrew Boyd may eventually acquire comparable standing. A seminal work can therefore have importance across a field without becoming a mandatory entry in every bibliography. This distinction separates scholarly stature from the narrower question of which sources a specific argument uses.

evidence.note: He names leading naval historians and describes seminal authors as generational reference points whose books remain excellent.

segments.title: How differences of perspective become book controversy
segments.summary: A small disagreement in interpretation can be marketed as a dramatic refutation, encouraging some historians to avoid invoking the landmark work at all.
segments.body: Citing a famous book while disagreeing with it can draw attention to a difference of interpretation. That difference may concern perspective or the weight assigned to evidence rather than a factual contradiction. A marketing team can still recast the nuance as a claim that the new book disproves a seminal work, because controversy attracts attention and sales. Such publicity can misrepresent the underlying scholarly disagreement. One way to avoid that publicity is to build the argument from primary sources and let the book stand on its own merits. Expected reception and publishing pressures can therefore affect citation choices.

evidence.note: He contrasts genuine evidentiary disagreement with differences of perspective that marketing can turn into drama.
He states his preference for avoiding that drama by returning to primary sources and letting the book stand alone.
